(2) FR Doc. 2026-20955 (Removal of Automatic Extensions for Certain Employment Authorization Documents) | Final Rule | Published October 14, 2026 (91 FR 65306) | Finalizes the Oct. 30, 2025 interim final rule ending up-to-540-day automatic EAD extensions under 8 CFR 274a.13(d)-(e) for EAD renewal applications filed on or after Oct. 30, 2025 in covered categories (while leaving intact the separate 180-day STEM OPT extension at 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv)). | In force (effective October 14, 2026). (3) FR Doc. 2026-19554 (Proclamation 11069, Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) | Presidential Document (Proclamation) | Published September 23, 2026 (91 FR 60497; signed Sept. 18, 2026) | Extends for 12 months (effective Sept. 21, 2026 through Sept. 21, 2027) the entry restriction and $100,000 payment requirement for H-1B specialty occupation workers outside the U.S. or requiring admission/consular processing to effectuate an H-1B petition. | In force (effective September 21, 2026 through September 21, 2027). (4) FR Doc. 2026-19555 (Executive Order 14431, Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program) | Presidential Document (Executive Order) | Published September 23, 2026 (91 FR 60501; signed Sept. 18, 2026) | Directs DHS, DOL, and State to coordinate with Commerce, Education, and SBA and consider whether a prospective H-1B employer has conducted or plans layoffs affecting U.S. workers when adjudicating LCAs, H-1B petitions, visas, and entries. | In force (signed September 18, 2026). (5) FR Doc. 2026-17324 (Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions, corrected by C1-2026-17324) | Proposed Rule | Published August 25, 2026 (91 FR 54817; correction Sept. 10, 2026, 91 FR 57516) | Proposes adding a $103,265 USCIS filing fee to all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including advanced-degree exemption petitions (while excluding cap-exempt employers). | Not in force (proposed rule; comments closed Sept. 24, 2026). (6) FR Doc. 2026-18631 (Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period) | Proposed Rule | Published September 11, 2026 (91 FR 57807) | Proposes removing 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) so workers in H-1B, O-1, TN, L-1, and E classifications lose the up-to-60-day grace period upon early cessation of employment. | Not in force (proposed rule; comments closed Nov. 10, 2026). (7) FR Doc. 2026-16231 (9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for H-1B and L-1 Visas) | Final Rule | Published August 10, 2026 (91 FR 51360) | Requires covered employers (50+ U.S. employees with >50% in H-1B/L-1 status) to pay the $4,000 H-1B 9-11 Biometric Fee on all H-1B extension-of-status petitions as well as initial grants and employer changes through September 30, 2027. | In force (effective September 9, 2026). (8) FR Doc. 2026-20941 (Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility) | Proposed Rule | Published October 14, 2026 (91 FR 65119) | Proposes removing 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) so USCIS no longer gives deference to prior petition/stay approvals involving the same facts when adjudicating extensions of employment-based petitions or stays. | Not in force (proposed rule; comments closed Nov. 13, 2026).

Q11.answer: On cost: The final regulatory text (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)) requires paying "the required fee" / "the appropriate fee" without stating a dollar figure. In the preamble, DHS does not state a specific Form I-539 filing fee amount in its own voice in the discussion, instead referring to "Table 16, Applicant Unit Costs for Filing an EOS with USCIS of the final Regulatory Impact Analysis" (91 FR 45082, available in the docket rather than printed in the FR). However, commenters stated that a Form I-539 EOS requires a $420 fee (91 FR 45055) and that four EOS filings would cost approximately $1,680 (91 FR 45082). DHS also reported an average legal-assistance cost of $490 (applied to 24.5% of applicants—70% paper filers times 35% needing assistance—based on the Form I-539 Supporting Statement, 91 FR 45083 & n.275), noted that dependents included via Form I-539A on the principal's Form I-539 require only one fee whereas a separate Form I-539 requires a separate fee (91 FR 45013, 45110), and estimated DSO processing costs at $233 per EOS request (91 FR 45092). On processing time: In the preamble (Section IV.Q.2.c(1), 91 FR 45084 & n.277), DHS stated that "80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications for F, M, and J aliens are completed in three months" (citing USCIS Case Processing Times as of February 23, 2026), while also stating repeatedly that DHS "cannot guarantee processing times for applications filed at USCIS" (91 FR 45025, 45029) and acknowledging past backlogs (DHS also noted USCIS's average EAD processing time is 60-120 days for foreign students, 91 FR 45032, 45107). Commenters reported I-539 processing times of 3.5 months at the California Service Center (91 FR 44999, 45083), 6 to 19 months (91 FR 45051), and 12 to 18 months during peak backlogs (91 FR 45031, 45036, 45048), and noted no expedited/premium processing exists for Form I-539 (91 FR 45031, 45051). DHS encourages filing EOS applications within 6 months (180 days) before stay expires (91 FR 45043, 45106-45107, 45110). Draft handout sentences: "To extend your F-1 stay, you must file Form I-539 with USCIS and pay the required filing fee (commenters in the rulemaking cited a $420 fee, though you should verify the current USCIS fee schedule; eligible F-2 dependents included on your application via Form I-539A do not pay a separate filing fee). DHS reports that 80% of Form I-539 applications for F, M, and J students/visitors have been decided within three months, but USCIS cannot guarantee processing times and past backlogs have been longer, so we encourage applying up to six months before your authorized stay expires."
Q11.uncertainty: Table 16 of the final Regulatory Impact Analysis (referenced at 91 FR 45082) is in the regulations.gov docket and not printed in the Federal Register, and DHS did not state the current Form I-539 online vs. paper filing fee in its own voice in the final rule text (so the $420 figure rests on commenter statements in the preamble rather than a USCIS fee table in 2026-14439).

Q12.answer: (a) Yes, it is timely. Under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (91 FR 45123), Priya's authorized period of stay is her May 15, 2027 program end date plus her 60-day departure period (through July 14, 2027). Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) (91 FR 45126) and 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4), an EOS application received by USCIS on or before the expiration of the student's authorized period of stay (including the departure period) is timely filed. (b) No. Under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (91 FR 45123), any authorized employment or training for D/S transition students continues only until the Form I-20 program end date (May 15, 2027). Furthermore, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) (91 FR 45125-45126) expressly state that an F-1 student who files an EOS application during the departure period does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment—including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship employment—and must wait until USCIS approves the EOS application (and any required EAD) before engaging in CPT or employment. Recommendation to the adviser: Advise Priya to file her Form I-539 (with her new master's Form I-20) on or before May 15, 2027 (ideally as early as possible, up to 6 months before expiration) if she has any eligible on-campus or CPT employment she seeks to continue uninterrupted, and in any event ensure USCIS receives the filing on or before July 14, 2027 (noting also that on-campus/CPT employment for a new program at a new school cannot begin before that program's authorized window and DSO/EOS authorization).
Q12.uncertainty: None (noting a minor textual mismatch: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) and (f)(7)(iii)(B) refer to "the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)" whereas D/S transition students like Priya receive a 60-day departure period under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1); either way, authorized employment ends on May 15, 2027 and automatic employment extension is unavailable if the EOS is filed during the departure period).

Q13.answer: (a) After her January 9, 2027 readmission, Sofia is authorized to remain until June 13, 2027 without filing anything. Provisions: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii) (preamble 91 FR 45017, 45101), 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) (91 FR 45122-45125). When she departed and was readmitted on January 9, 2027, she transitioned out of D/S to a fixed admission period equal to her Form I-20 program end date (May 14, 2027) plus 30 days (not 60 days). Arithmetic: May 14, 2027 + 30 days = 17 remaining days in May (May 15-31) + 13 days in June = June 13, 2027. (b) Yes, she must file a Form I-539 (EOS) in addition to Form I-765. Under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii) (91 FR 45123), a D/S transition student who departs the U.S. before filing for post-completion OPT and is readmitted with a fixed period of admission must file both Form I-765 and Form I-539 pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) (even though she files on February 22, 2027, prior to March 18, 2027). Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) (and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)), USCIS must receive Form I-539 on or before the expiration of her authorized period of stay, including the 30-day departure period—i.e., on or before June 13, 2027. (c) If everything is approved as requested (OPT through June 9, 2028), under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D), (f)(7)(vi), and (f)(5)(v) (91 FR 45125-45127), her approved stay includes an additional 30-day departure period after June 9, 2028: 21 remaining days in June (June 10-30) + 9 days in July = July 9, 2028. (d) Under the alternative facts (no December travel; Form I-765 filed February 22, 2027; trips May 20 to June 5, 2027 while I-765 is pending): she does not need to file a Form I-539. Because she filed Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 without having previously departed and shifted to a fixed date, she qualifies for the transition exemption in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123); under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii), (m)(1)(ii) (second sentence), and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D), departing while the I-765 is pending does not abandon the I-765 and she instead seeks admission through CBP under 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii). At re-entry on June 5, 2027, under 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii) (91 FR 45122), CBP may admit her until the DSO's recommended OPT end date on Form I-20 (June 9, 2028) plus 30 days under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) = July 9, 2028. Under 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii) and (c)(8)(iii) (91 FR 45122-45123; preamble 91 FR 45098), she should carry her Form I-797C receipt notice for the pending Form I-765 and her latest Form I-20 endorsed by the DSO for OPT with the proposed end date (along with valid passport and F-1 visa unless exempt/automatic revalidation).
Q13.uncertainty: In (d), CBP admission at a port of entry is discretionary ("may be admitted," 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)), and footnote 303 in the preamble (91 FR 45100) notes ICE guidance cautioning against travel while OPT is pending (e.g., risk of missing an RFE or EAD delivery); additionally, if she returned via contiguous territory under automatic visa revalidation (8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)) rather than full inspection, admission is limited to the prior unexpired period.

Q14.answer: (a) The document is "Optional Practical Training Fees," FR Doc. 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566 (pages 64566-64600), Proposed Rule (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking / NPRM), issued by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Department of Homeland Security (DHS); Docket No. DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01; published October 8, 2026. Current status and deadlines: proposed rule (not in force); general public comments were due on or before November 9, 2026 (closed as of Nov. 14, 2026); Paperwork Reduction Act (information collection) comments are due on or before December 7, 2026; and the proposed effective date is 60 days after publication of a final rule in the Federal Register (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), 91 FR 64577, 64600). (b) If finalized as proposed and in effect before the DSO's April 2027 recommendation, the $70,000 fee—not $30,000—would apply to Daniel's STEM OPT extension. Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3) (91 FR 64600; preamble 91 FR 64577), the $30,000 subsequent fee applies only "if the alien has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000," and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3) requires schools recommending "any type of OPT" on or after the effective date to pay $70,000 for any student for whom the $70,000 initial OPT fee has not yet been paid. Because Daniel received his initial post-completion OPT in 2026 before the proposed rule, the $70,000 fee was never paid for him. (c) Under the proposal: the SEVP-certified educational institution (Daniel's school) must pay the fee (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2), 214.2(f)(11)(ii)); payment must be made prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation in SEVIS and issuing the recommendation to the student, and before the student applies to USCIS (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(B)-(C), 214.13(i)(1)-(2)); if payment is not made beforehand, the DSO may not enter the recommendation in SEVIS and USCIS "may not grant employment authorization" to the student (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii), 91 FR 64599). Refundability: SEVP has case-by-case discretion to grant a school's refund request (after the DSO removes the SEVIS recommendation) only if the student has not been issued/granted the OPT EAD (and refund denials are not appealable); once the EAD is issued/granted, the fee "will not be refunded under any circumstances" (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2), 91 FR 64600). (d) Under proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3) (91 FR 64600), the fee applies to any F-1 student who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT dated on or after the final rule's effective date (60 days after final rule publication). Yes: if the DSO issues the STEM OPT recommendation dated before the final rule's effective date (consistent with existing 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C) timing rules, which allow filing up to 90 days before the June 30, 2027 EAD expires—i.e., starting April 1, 2027—and within 60 days of the DSO recommendation), Daniel would be outside the fee. (e) Under the rules in force today: because Daniel plans to file on April 12, 2027—after the March 18, 2027 cutoff for the Form I-539 transition exemption in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)—he must file both Form I-765 and Form I-539 (EOS) with USCIS (unless DHS publishes a Federal Register notice extending the exemption under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)), pursuant to 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A). Work authorization while pending: under 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C)—which 2026-14439 left unchanged (91 FR 45002, 45037, 45101) and which 2026-20955 (91 FR 65306) did not alter—if Daniel timely files for STEM OPT before June 30, 2027, his employment authorization is automatically extended for up to 180 days after June 30, 2027 (until USCIS's written decision or December 27, 2027, whichever is earlier; arithmetic: 31 days in July + 31 in Aug + 30 in Sept + 31 in Oct + 30 in Nov = 153 days + 27 days in Dec = Dec 27, 2027). If both are approved (24-month STEM OPT ending June 30, 2029), under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi) and (f)(5)(v) he may stay until June 30, 2029 plus 30 days = July 30, 2029 (note: only those exempt under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) receive 60 days).
Q14.uncertainty: In (e), there is a minor tension between preamble passages in 2026-14439: at 91 FR 45002 and 45037, DHS states that students timely filing for STEM OPT retain the 180-day automatic EAD extension under 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) (and remain in status if they timely filed EOS), whereas a sentence at 91 FR 45024 states students may begin or continue OPT employment only after both EOS and EAD are approved unless qualifying for transition relief; the specific regulatory text of 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) was not amended by either 2026-14439 or 2026-20955 and controls. Also, DHS could still exercise 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii) before March 18, 2027 to extend the Form I-539 exemption.

Q15.answer: 1. Incorrect. Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) (91 FR 45126), an EOS is timely if USCIS receives it on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, which includes the 30-day departure period under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) (or 60 days for D/S transition students under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)); however, filing during the departure period forfeits the automatic extension of on-campus/CPT/severe economic hardship employment (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(iii)(B)). Rewording: "USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application on or before the student's authorized stay expires (including the 30-day departure period, or 60 days for D/S transition students), though to keep an automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment while it is pending, USCIS must receive it before the program end date." 2. Incorrect. Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) (91 FR 45124) and preamble at 91 FR 45016 and 45098, the 30-day arrival window before the program start date does not count toward the 4-year maximum; the 4-year period is counted from the program start date. Rewording: "The four-year maximum period of admission is counted from the program start date on the Form I-20, not from the day the student enters during the 30-day pre-program arrival window." 3. Correct (for a student who timely filed the EOS before the 30-day departure period began). Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) (91 FR 45125-45126) and preamble (91 FR 45106), the student remains in authorized stay and may keep studying until USCIS decides the EOS, while automatic extension of on-campus employment is capped at 240 days after the Form I-94 admit-until date. Rewording (for precision): "If USCIS has still not decided an extension application (filed before the 30-day departure period began) 240 days after the Form I-94 admit-until date, the student may stay and keep studying but must stop any on-campus job until the extension is approved." 4. Incorrect (noting preamble confirmation of the text). Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A) (91 FR 45124), ELT students are restricted to a maximum admission period of 24 months (plus 30 days to depart), and the preamble at 91 FR 45039 explicitly states that "[s]tudents who encounter extenuating circumstances such as illness, disability, or other emergencies during their studies, will still be limited to the 24-month admission period" (noting that while 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii) allows medical extensions generally and (f)(7)(vi) cites only the 4-year cap, the specific 24-month ELT cap in (f)(5)(i)(A) and preamble at 91 FR 45039, 45110 govern; D/S transition students already in ELT on Sept. 15, 2026 may finish their existing I-20 up to 4 years under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)). Rewording: "Students in standalone English language training programs are capped at 24 months total (plus 30 days to depart) and cannot extend beyond 24 months even for illness or medical emergencies." 5. Incorrect. Preamble at 91 FR 45039-45040 expressly calls this "untrue": a 5-year accredited program uses a single Form I-20 stating the full 5-year length, and the student applies for an EOS with USCIS under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (f)(7)(i)(C)(1) before the initial 4-year stay expires. Rewording: "A degree program accredited as a five-year program does not need to be shortened or split onto two Forms I-20; the school issues one Form I-20 for the full five-year program, and the student applies to USCIS for an extension of stay before the initial four-year admission period ends." 6. Partly correct. Under 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)-(B) (91 FR 45122) and preamble (91 FR 45025, 45098), CBP may admit a returning student on a valid Form I-20 with a later program end date for up to that end date (maximum 4 years plus 30 days), eliminating the need for a USCIS EOS for that new period; however, CBP admission is discretionary, the student must have a valid visa (or qualify for automatic revalidation) and be otherwise eligible (e.g., not barred by 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) or the 24-month ELT cap), and if an EOS was already pending, seeking admission on a new later program end date may cause USCIS to deem the pending EOS abandoned (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)). Rewording: "A student who travels abroad with a valid visa and Form I-20 showing a later program end date may, at CBP's discretion if otherwise eligible, be readmitted for up to that new end date (maximum four years plus 30 days) without needing a USCIS extension for that period—though if an extension application was already pending, seeking admission on the new end date may cause USCIS to deem the pending application abandoned." 7. Incorrect (and regulatory text diverges from preamble). Divergence: Several preamble passages describe the OPT/STEM OPT Form I-539 exemption as covering Form I-765 filings "within six months of the effective date" (91 FR 44978, 45033, 45034; six months from Sept. 15, 2026 would be March 15, 2027), whereas the final regulatory text at 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123)—along with other preamble passages (91 FR 45017, 45031, 45033, 45034)—specifically sets the cutoff date as "on or before March 18, 2027." The regulatory text controls, so the last filing day is March 18, 2027 (and the exemption applies only to D/S transition students who have not departed and been readmitted for a fixed period, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)). Rewording: "The transition exemption from filing Form I-539 for OPT and STEM OPT applicants applies to D/S transition students who have not departed and been readmitted for a fixed date and who timely file Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027."
Q15.uncertainty: None (the two textual tensions noted in statements 4 and 7 are resolved in favor of the specific ELT 24-month cap and the controlling regulatory date of March 18, 2027).

Q16.answer: (a) Lin's Form I-94 should show an admit-until date of September 22, 2031. Arithmetic: Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (f)(5)(v) (91 FR 45124-45125) and preamble (91 FR 45016, 45098), her August 2, 2027 entry within the 30-day pre-program window does not count toward the 4-year maximum; the 4-year maximum runs from her program start date (August 23, 2027) to August 23, 2031, plus an additional 30 days for departure preparation: 8 remaining days in August (Aug 24-31) + 22 days in September = September 22, 2031. (b) To stay beyond September 22, 2031, Lin must file an EOS application (Form I-539) with USCIS on or before September 22, 2031 (or before August 23, 2031 to preserve automatic extension of any on-campus/CPT employment) under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). She must submit the designated EOS form, required fee, her updated/properly endorsed Form I-20 showing the May 14, 2033 program end date, evidence of sufficient funds to cover expenses, and any biometrics required under 8 CFR 103.16 (along with proof of maintaining status and full-time study) (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)-(iii)). It can be granted under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1) based on "[a] currently issued Form I-20, or successor form, indicating additional time is left to complete his or her program of study" (preamble 91 FR 45040, 45108-45109 also references compelling academic reasons for standard programs exceeding 4 years). How early she may file: there is no regulatory prohibition on how early Form I-539 may be filed ahead of expiration (91 FR 45040 n.197, 45107 n.328, 45110 n.338), though DHS generally recommends filing within the 6 months preceding expiration (91 FR 45043, 45106-45107, 45110). If granted in full (through May 14, 2033), under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi) and (f)(5)(v) she may stay until May 14, 2033 plus 30 days: 17 remaining days in May (May 15-31) + 13 days in June = June 13, 2033. (c) No. In the preamble at 91 FR 45042-45043, DHS explicitly confirmed that a student issued a Form I-20 for a PhD program as the primary academic objective may obtain a master's degree incidental to status while progressing toward completing the PhD; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) bars only starting a new program at the same or lower level after completing a program. (d) When Lin departs and seeks readmission in August 2030 (with no EOS pending) on her valid Form I-20 showing May 14, 2033 (less than 4 years away), CBP may admit her under 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) (as explained in preamble at 91 FR 45098) up to her May 14, 2033 program end date plus 30 days = June 13, 2033; if CBP admits her through June 13, 2033, she would no longer need the EOS filing in (b). Certainty: Moderately certain, subject to three caveats: (1) CBP admission and exact admit-until period ("may be admitted" / "up to") are discretionary; (2) if her three-week trip is solely to contiguous territory or adjacent islands and she relies on automatic visa revalidation under 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1), CBP admits only up to the previously authorized unexpired stay (Sept. 22, 2031); and (3) textually, 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) refers to admission "after a previously authorized period of admission ... expired" while (i)(B) covers returns with a pending EOS, so returning without a pending EOS before prior stay expires relies on the preamble's explicit statement at 91 FR 45098 that returning aliens without an EOS may be admitted for the remaining I-20 length up to 4 years plus 30 days. (e) Even if her husband's I-94 shows a later date, he may stay only as long as Lin's authorized period of stay (September 22, 2031 unless/until Lin obtains a later authorized stay). Under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E) (91 FR 45124), an F-2 dependent's authorized stay may not exceed the principal F-1 student's authorized stay, and preamble at 91 FR 45016 confirms that dependents cannot stay longer than the principal even if the F-2's I-94 reflects a longer end date. When Lin applies under (b), under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv) (91 FR 45123, 45126), her husband may either be included on Lin's Form I-539 application (by filing Form I-539A) or file his own separate Form I-539 (with proof of relationship, maintenance of status, no unauthorized work, updated I-20, funds, and biometrics if required). On the fee: the preamble at 91 FR 45013 and 45110 states that if the dependent files Form I-539A as part of the principal's Form I-539 request, only one Form I-539 filing fee is required, whereas if the dependent files a separate Form I-539, a separate filing fee is required.
Q16.uncertainty: For (d), CBP's grant of a new full admission period upon re-entry is discretionary, depends on visa validity / not using 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1) automatic revalidation, and relies on the preamble at 91 FR 45098 rather than an explicit pre-expiration non-EOS clause in 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)-(B).
